questions.question: A circle graph shows how 200 students at a Surrey school travel to school: Walk 40%, Bus 25%, Car 20%, Bike 15%. How many students walk to school?
options: 40 students
50 students
80 students
8 students
questions.explain: A percent of the circle means that percent of the total, so 40% of 200 = 0.40 × 200 = 80 students. The most common trap is copying the number 40 straight from the slice label — 40 is the percent, not the number of students.

questions.question: When drawing a circle graph, a slice must show 25% of the data. What central angle should that slice have?
questions.explain: A whole circle is 360°, so a slice angle is that percent of 360°: 25% of 360° = 90°. Two common traps are writing 25° (using the percent as the angle) and using 180° instead of 360° as the whole circle, which gives 45°.

questions.question: Which set of data is best displayed in a circle graph?
options: The snowfall at Whistler on each of seven days last week.
The height of four different trees in a Burnaby park.
The temperature outside Ella's window every hour from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.
How a Grade 7 class divided its $600 fundraiser among four school clubs.
questions.explain: A circle graph is for showing how one whole is split into parts, and the $600 is one whole divided among four clubs. The trap is choosing data that changes over time (snowfall, hourly temperature) — those are line graph data, and comparing separate amounts like tree heights belongs in a bar graph.

questions.question: A circle graph shows the favourite winter activity of 480 students in Nanaimo: Skating 35%, Swimming 30%, Hiking 20%, Skiing 15%. How many more students chose skating than swimming?
options: 24 students
5 students
48 students
168 students
questions.explain: Find each amount first: 35% of 480 = 168 and 30% of 480 = 144, so the difference is 24 students (or take the 5% difference of 480 directly). The common trap is answering 5, which is the difference in percents, not in students.

questions.question: A class of 40 students chose a lunch for a field trip: pizza 10, sushi 8, sandwich 14, salad 8. On a circle graph of this data, what central angle should the sandwich slice have?
questions.explain: Turn the count into a fraction of the whole, then into an angle: 14/40 × 360° = 126° (or 360° ÷ 40 = 9° per student, then 14 × 9° = 126°). Traps are stopping at the percent (35) and calling it degrees, and reading the wrong scale on the protractor, which gives the reflex angle 234°.

questions.question: Sofia recorded how many books her class read in each month from September to June, then drew a circle graph of the ten monthly totals. Why is a circle graph a poor choice for this data?
options: Because a circle graph can only show four categories at a time.
Because the months are steps in time, so a line graph would show the trend and let her predict the next month.
Because circle graphs must use fractions, and book counts are whole numbers.
Because a circle graph cannot be drawn accurately without a protractor.
questions.explain: Circle graphs answer how big is each part of one whole, so they hide any trend over time — for month-by-month data a line graph shows rises, drops, and predictions. The trap is thinking the problem is the number of categories; a circle graph can have ten slices, it just should not be used for a sequence in time.

questions.question: Riverside School has 300 students and its circle graph shows 40% bike to school. Cedar School has 600 students and its circle graph shows 30% bike to school. Which school has more students who bike?
options: Cedar School — 30% of 600 is 180 riders, more than 40% of 300, which is 120.
Riverside School — 40% is a bigger percent than 30%, so it must have more riders.
Riverside School — 40% of 600 is 240 riders, more than 30% of 300, which is 90.
They are equal — each circle graph is one whole, so equal-looking slices stand for equal numbers.
questions.explain: A percent is always a percent of that graph's own total, so compare actual counts: 40% of 300 = 120 riders and 30% of 600 = 180 riders, making Cedar School larger. The classic trap is comparing the percents alone — a bigger percent of a smaller whole can be fewer students.

questions.question: 90 students went to the winter carnival. The table shows: Bus 30, Car 24, Bike 15, and everyone else walked. Liam is drawing a circle graph. What central angle should the walking slice have?
questions.explain: First find the missing count: 90 − (30 + 24 + 15) = 21 walkers; then 360° ÷ 90 = 4° per student, so 21 × 4° = 84°. Two traps are using the count 21 as the angle, and forgetting the missing category so that the leftover slice gets the car angle of 96° instead.
